en.userdoc.certs.intro: kcore uses mutual TLS (mTLS) for all management-plane communication. Disk encryption with LUKS2 protects data at rest.

en.userdoc.certs.luks.li2: Key-file path — passphrase-based unlock using a key file.

en.userdoc.certs.renewal.p: The node-agent checks certificate expiry daily. If a certificate expires within 30 days, the agent calls the RenewNodeCert RPC. The sub-CA signs a new leaf certificate and returns the updated chain.
en.userdoc.certs.rotation.p: rotate sub-ca generates a new sub-CA and pushes it to the controller. rotate certs re-signs the controller certificate and triggers ReloadTls on the controller.
en.userdoc.certs.tls.li1: Production — mTLS required (default). All gRPC and API traffic is encrypted and mutually authenticated.
en.userdoc.certs.tls.li2: Development — kctl --insecure disables TLS for local testing over plain HTTP.

en.userdoc.storage.intro: kcore supports three VM data-plane storage backends: filesystem, LVM, and ZFS. The backend is chosen at node install time and determines where VM disks are stored.
en.userdoc.storage.luksEncryptionP1: The OS disk is always encrypted with LUKS2. When /sys/class/tpm/tpm0 exists on the node, the key is TPM2-sealed for automatic unlock on boot. Otherwise a key-file is used.
en.userdoc.storage.luksEncryptionP2: The recovery key is written to /etc/kcore/recovery/luks-recovery-key.txt (root-only, mode 0400). Store this key securely — it is the only way to unlock the disk if the TPM is cleared or the key-file is lost.

en.userdoc.storagevsan.complementsLocalP1: Local backends (filesystem, LVM, ZFS) remain the right choice for single-node, performance-sensitive workloads where raw I/O throughput matters most. vSAN is designed for workloads that prioritise availability over raw I/O performance.

en.userdoc.vxlan.addressing.p: The controller allocates IPs starting at .2 within the subnet, incrementing monotonically. IPs are not reclaimed when a VM is deleted. Addresses are assigned to VMs via cloud-init static network configuration, not DHCP.
en.userdoc.vxlan.dataplane.p: Each VXLAN network creates a Linux VXLAN device (vxlan<VNI>) using UDP port 4789. The VXLAN device is attached to a bridge (kbr-<name>), and the gateway IP is assigned to the bridge interface to serve as the subnet gateway.
en.userdoc.vxlan.firewall.p: All kbr-* bridges are treated as trusted interfaces in the node firewall. UDP port 4789 is automatically allowed when any VXLAN network exists on the node.
en.userdoc.vxlan.intro: VXLAN overlays provide L2 connectivity across multiple nodes, allowing VMs on different hosts to communicate on the same logical network.
en.userdoc.vxlan.nat.p: Outbound internet access for VMs on VXLAN networks is optional. Enable it with --enable-outbound-nat (or omit --no-outbound-nat) when creating the network. When enabled, kcore adds an nftables masquerade rule on the gateway interface so that VMs can reach external destinations.
en.userdoc.vxlan.optout.p: Pass --disable-vxlan during node installation to prevent VXLAN network creation on that node. NAT and bridge networks continue to work normally. If a VXLAN network creation is attempted on a node with VXLAN disabled, the controller returns a FailedPrecondition error.
en.userdoc.vxlan.peers.p2: This implements head-end replication (flood-to-peers): BUM traffic is replicated to every known peer.

it.userdoc.storage.intro: kcore supports three VM data-plane storage backends: filesystem, LVM, and ZFS. The backend is chosen at node install time and determines where VM disks are stored.
it.userdoc.storage.luksEncryptionP1: The OS disk is always encrypted with LUKS2. When /sys/class/tpm/tpm0 exists on the node, the key is TPM2-sealed for automatic unlock on boot. Otherwise a key-file is used.
it.userdoc.storage.luksEncryptionP2: The recovery key is written to /etc/kcore/recovery/luks-recovery-key.txt (root-only, mode 0400). Store this key securely — it is the only way to unlock the disk if the TPM is cleared or the key-file is lost.

it.userdoc.storage.tdLvmDesc: Disko creates the PV and VG at install time. The node-agent creates and deletes LVs at runtime via lvcreate. The VG name is configurable (default vg_kcore).

it.userdoc.storage.tdZfsDesc: Disko creates the pool at install time. The node-agent uses it for zvol and dataset operations. The pool name is configurable (default tank0).

it.userdoc.storagevsan.complementsLocalP1: Local backends (filesystem, LVM, ZFS) remain the right choice for single-node, performance-sensitive workloads where raw I/O throughput matters most. vSAN is designed for workloads that prioritise availability over raw I/O performance.
it.userdoc.storagevsan.complementsLocalP2: Operators choose per-VM: a database that needs low-latency local NVMe stays on LVM, while a stateless application server uses Ceph-backed storage for easy failover.
it.userdoc.storagevsan.integrationLi1: Ceph OSDs deployed on data disks at install time using a new --storage-backend ceph flag.
it.userdoc.storagevsan.integrationLi2: Controller manages pool topology and replication factor.
it.userdoc.storagevsan.integrationLi3: RBD volumes created and attached as VM disks transparently.
it.userdoc.storagevsan.integrationLi4: CRUSH map aligned with DC topology (dc_id) so replicas span failure domains.
it.userdoc.storagevsan.intro: kcore currently supports local storage backends (filesystem, LVM, ZFS) where VM disks live on the host running the VM. vSAN will add distributed shared storage using Ceph, enabling VM disks to be replicated across nodes.

it.userdoc.vxlan.addressing.p: The controller allocates IPs starting at .2 within the subnet, incrementing monotonically. IPs are not reclaimed when a VM is deleted. Addresses are assigned to VMs via cloud-init static network configuration, not DHCP.
it.userdoc.vxlan.dataplane.p: Each VXLAN network creates a Linux VXLAN device (vxlan<VNI>) using UDP port 4789. The VXLAN device is attached to a bridge (kbr-<name>), and the gateway IP is assigned to the bridge interface to serve as the subnet gateway.
it.userdoc.vxlan.firewall.p: All kbr-* bridges are treated as trusted interfaces in the node firewall. UDP port 4789 is automatically allowed when any VXLAN network exists on the node.
it.userdoc.vxlan.intro: VXLAN overlays provide L2 connectivity across multiple nodes, allowing VMs on different hosts to communicate on the same logical network.
it.userdoc.vxlan.nat.p: Outbound internet access for VMs on VXLAN networks is optional. Enable it with --enable-outbound-nat (or omit --no-outbound-nat) when creating the network. When enabled, kcore adds an nftables masquerade rule on the gateway interface so that VMs can reach external destinations.
it.userdoc.vxlan.optout.p: Pass --disable-vxlan during node installation to prevent VXLAN network creation on that node. NAT and bridge networks continue to work normally. If a VXLAN network creation is attempted on a node with VXLAN disabled, the controller returns a FailedPrecondition error.

fr.userdoc.vxlan.dataplane.p: Each VXLAN network creates a Linux VXLAN device (vxlan<VNI>) using UDP port 4789. The VXLAN device is attached to a bridge (kbr-<name>), and the gateway IP is assigned to the bridge interface to serve as the subnet gateway.
fr.userdoc.vxlan.firewall.p: All kbr-* bridges are treated as trusted interfaces in the node firewall. UDP port 4789 is automatically allowed when any VXLAN network exists on the node.
fr.userdoc.vxlan.intro: VXLAN overlays provide L2 connectivity across multiple nodes, allowing VMs on different hosts to communicate on the same logical network.
fr.userdoc.vxlan.nat.p: Outbound internet access for VMs on VXLAN networks is optional. Enable it with --enable-outbound-nat (or omit --no-outbound-nat) when creating the network. de.userdoc.vxlan.addressing.p: The controller allocates IPs starting at .2 within the subnet, incrementing monotonically. IPs are not reclaimed when a VM is deleted. Addresses are assigned to VMs via cloud-init static network configuration, not DHCP.
de.userdoc.vxlan.dataplane.p: Each VXLAN network creates a Linux VXLAN device (vxlan<VNI>) using UDP port 4789. The VXLAN device is attached to a bridge (kbr-<name>), and the gateway IP is assigned to the bridge interface to serve as the subnet gateway.
de.userdoc.vxlan.firewall.p: All kbr-* bridges are treated as trusted interfaces in the node firewall. UDP port 4789 is automatically allowed when any VXLAN network exists on the node.
de.userdoc.vxlan.intro: VXLAN overlays provide L2 connectivity across multiple nodes, allowing VMs on different hosts to communicate on the same logical network.
de.userdoc.vxlan.nat.p: Outbound internet access for VMs on VXLAN networks is optional. Enable it with --enable-outbound-nat (or omit --no-outbound-nat) when creating the network. When enabled, kcore adds an nftables masquerade rule on the gateway interface so that VMs can reach external destinations.
de.userdoc.vxlan.optout.p: Pass --disable-vxlan during node installation to prevent VXLAN network creation on that node. NAT and bridge networks continue to work normally. If a VXLAN network creation is attempted on a node with VXLAN disabled, the controller returns a FailedPrecondition error.

pt.userdoc.vxlan.addressing.p: The controller allocates IPs starting at .2 within the subnet, incrementing monotonically. IPs are not reclaimed when a VM is deleted. Addresses are assigned to VMs via cloud-init static network configuration, not DHCP.
pt.userdoc.vxlan.dataplane.p: Each VXLAN network creates a Linux VXLAN device (vxlan<VNI>) using UDP port 4789. The VXLAN device is attached to a bridge (kbr-<name>), and the gateway IP is assigned to the bridge interface to serve as the subnet gateway.
pt.userdoc.vxlan.firewall.p: All kbr-* bridges are treated as trusted interfaces in the node firewall. UDP port 4789 is automatically allowed when any VXLAN network exists on the node.
pt.userdoc.vxlan.intro: VXLAN overlays provide L2 connectivity across multiple nodes, allowing VMs on different hosts to communicate on the same logical network.
pt.userdoc.vxlan.nat.p: Outbound internet access for VMs on VXLAN networks is optional. Enable it with --enable-outbound-nat (or omit --no-outbound-nat) when creating the network. When enabled, kcore adds an nftables masquerade rule on the gateway interface so that VMs can reach external destinations.
pt.userdoc.vxlan.optout.p: Pass --disable-vxlan during node installation to prevent VXLAN network creation on that node. NAT and bridge networks continue to work normally. If a VXLAN network creation is attempted on a node with VXLAN disabled, the controller returns a FailedPrecondition error.
pt.userdoc.vxlan.peers.p2: This implements head-end replication (flood-to-peers): BUM traffic is replicated to every known peer.

ja.userdoc.vxlan.addressing.p: The controller allocates IPs starting at .2 within the subnet, incrementing monotonically. IPs are not reclaimed when a VM is deleted. Addresses are assigned to VMs via cloud-init static network configuration, not DHCP.
ja.userdoc.vxlan.dataplane.p: Each VXLAN network creates a Linux VXLAN device (vxlan<VNI>) using UDP port 4789. The VXLAN device is attached to a bridge (kbr-<name>), and the gateway IP is assigned to the bridge interface to serve as the subnet gateway.
ja.userdoc.vxlan.firewall.p: All kbr-* bridges are treated as trusted interfaces in the node firewall. UDP port 4789 is automatically allowed when any VXLAN network exists on the node.
ja.userdoc.vxlan.intro: VXLAN overlays provide L2 connectivity across multiple nodes, allowing VMs on different hosts to communicate on the same logical network.
ja.userdoc.vxlan.nat.p: Outbound internet access for VMs on VXLAN networks is optional. Enable it with --enable-outbound-nat (or omit --no-outbound-nat) when creating the network. When enabled, kcore adds an nftables masquerade rule on the gateway interface so that VMs can reach external destinations.
ja.userdoc.vxlan.optout.p: Pass --disable-vxlan during node installation to prevent VXLAN network creation on that node. NAT and bridge networks continue to work normally. If a VXLAN network creation is attempted on a node with VXLAN disabled, the controller returns a FailedPrecondition error.
ja.userdoc.vxlan.peers.p2: This implements head-end replication (flood-to-peers): BUM traffic is replicated to every known peer.

zh.userdoc.certs.bootstrap.p: kctl create cluster generates the full PKI (root CA, sub-CA, controller cert, kctl client cert). kctl node install pushes the node certificate, private key, and CA chain to the target node. Controller nodes also receive the sub-CA key pair.
zh.userdoc.certs.inspect.p: kctl get nodes shows cert_expiry_days per node. The compliance report includes a Certificate Lifecycle section with expiring and unknown certificate counts.
zh.userdoc.certs.intro: kcore uses mutual TLS (mTLS) for all management-plane communication. Disk encryption with LUKS2 protects data at rest.
zh.userdoc.certs.luks.li1: TPM2 path — systemd-cryptenroll seals the LUKS key to the TPM2 device.
zh.userdoc.certs.luks.li2: Key-file path — passphrase-based unlock using a key file.
zh.userdoc.certs.luks.p: LUKS2 encryption is mandatory for the OS disk on every node.
zh.userdoc.certs.luksreport.p: The node-agent detects the LUKS unlock method at registration: tpm2 if /dev/mapper/cryptroot exists and a TPM device is present, key-file otherwise. kctl get compliance-report shows the cluster-wide LUKS breakdown by method.
zh.userdoc.certs.pki.li2: Sub-CA — lives on the controller, signs node leaf certificates
zh.userdoc.certs.pki.li3: Controller cert — identifies the controller to nodes and clients
zh.userdoc.certs.renewal.p: The node-agent checks certificate expiry daily. If a certificate expires within 30 days, the agent calls the RenewNodeCert RPC. The sub-CA signs a new leaf certificate and returns the updated chain.
zh.userdoc.certs.rotation.p: rotate sub-ca generates a new sub-CA and pushes it to the controller. rotate certs re-signs the controller certificate and triggers ReloadTls on the controller.
zh.userdoc.certs.tls.li1: Production — mTLS required (default). All gRPC and API traffic is encrypted and mutually authenticated.
zh.userdoc.certs.tls.li2: Development — kctl --insecure disables TLS for local testing over plain HTTP.
zh.userdoc.certs.tls.note: Never use --insecure in production. Disabling mTLS removes authentication and encryption from the management plane.

zh.userdoc.compliance.certlife.p: Sub-CA enabled, auto-renewal window (30 days), expiring and unknown certificate counts. Maps to SOC 2 CC6.1, PCI 3.6.
zh.userdoc.compliance.crypto.p: Library: aws-lc-rs / AWS-LC (FIPS 140-3 certificate #4816). TLS 1.3 and TLS 1.2 cipher suites, key-exchange groups, and excluded algorithms are enumerated. Maps to FIPS 140-3, PCI DSS 4.2, SOC 2 CC6.1.

zh.userdoc.storage.intro: kcore supports three VM data-plane storage backends: filesystem, LVM, and ZFS. The backend is chosen at node install time and determines where VM disks are stored.
zh.userdoc.storage.luksEncryptionP1: The OS disk is always encrypted with LUKS2. When /sys/class/tpm/tpm0 exists on the node, the key is TPM2-sealed for automatic unlock on boot. Otherwise a key-file is used.
zh.userdoc.storage.luksEncryptionP2: The recovery key is written to /etc/kcore/recovery/luks-recovery-key.txt (root-only, mode 0400). Store this key securely — it is the only way to unlock the disk if the TPM is cleared or the key-file is lost.

zh.userdoc.storagevsan.complementsLocalP1: Local backends (filesystem, LVM, ZFS) remain the right choice for single-node, performance-sensitive workloads where raw I/O throughput matters most. vSAN is designed for workloads that prioritise availability over raw I/O performance.
zh.userdoc.storagevsan.complementsLocalP2: Operators choose per-VM: a database that needs low-latency local NVMe stays on LVM, while a stateless application server uses Ceph-backed storage for easy failover.

zh.userdoc.vxlan.addressing.p: The controller allocates IPs starting at .2 within the subnet, incrementing monotonically. IPs are not reclaimed when a VM is deleted. Addresses are assigned to VMs via cloud-init static network configuration, not DHCP.
zh.userdoc.vxlan.dataplane.p: Each VXLAN network creates a Linux VXLAN device (vxlan<VNI>) using UDP port 4789. The VXLAN device is attached to a bridge (kbr-<name>), and the gateway IP is assigned to the bridge interface to serve as the subnet gateway.
zh.userdoc.vxlan.firewall.p: All kbr-* bridges are treated as trusted interfaces in the node firewall. UDP port 4789 is automatically allowed when any VXLAN network exists on the node.
zh.userdoc.vxlan.intro: VXLAN overlays provide L2 connectivity across multiple nodes, allowing VMs on different hosts to communicate on the same logical network.
zh.userdoc.vxlan.nat.p: Outbound internet access for VMs on VXLAN networks is optional. Enable it with --enable-outbound-nat (or omit --no-outbound-nat) when creating the network. When enabled, kcore adds an nftables masquerade rule on the gateway interface so that VMs can reach external destinations.
zh.userdoc.vxlan.optout.p: Pass --disable-vxlan during node installation to prevent VXLAN network creation on that node. NAT and bridge networks continue to work normally. If a VXLAN network creation is attempted on a node with VXLAN disabled, the controller returns a FailedPrecondition error.
zh.userdoc.vxlan.peers.p2: This implements head-end replication (flood-to-peers): BUM traffic is replicated to every known peer.
